Theorem (1 + 1.8) on the Goldbach conjecture

Ruiyi Zhang Independent Researcher, Columbia, Maryland, USA
Abstract.

Every sufficiently large even integer NN has a representation N=p+r⁢qN=p+rq. Here p,qp,q are primes and rr is 11 or a prime, with r≤qa−1=q4/5=q0.8r\leq q^{a-1}=q^{4/5}=q^{0.8}. This is Proposition (1+a)(1+a) of Li–Liu with a=1.8=9/5a=1.8=9/5. We use a weighted sieve on shifted primes. Its level of distribution exceeds one half. The proof combines thirteen row estimates with a switched upper bound. For a fixed source cutoff, the certified D-unit endpoint is Dlower=1.83399665352036682372D_{\rm lower}=1.83399665352036682372. Since the source mass is 4⁢(1−εA)⁢UC4(1-\varepsilon_{A})U_{C}, division by four gives (1−εA)⁢Dlower=1.833813253855014787037628−o⁢(1)(1-\varepsilon_{A})D_{\rm lower}=1.833813253855014787037628-o(1). The balanced-semiprime cost is at most 1.788209644611262112809348242339+o⁢(1)1.788209644611262112809348242339+o(1) in those units. The remaining coefficient is 0.04560360924375267422827−o⁢(1)0.04560360924375267422827-o(1).

Key words and phrases:
Goldbach problem, almost-primes, sieve methods, well-factorable weights, shifted primes

1. Introduction

Chen announced his theorem in 1966 [1]. His proof appeared in 1973 [2]. By this theorem, every sufficiently large even integer is a prime plus an integer with at most two prime factors. Li and Liu [6] formulate Proposition (1+a)(1+a):

N=p+r⁢q,p,q∈ℙ,r∈{1}∪ℙ,r≤qa−1.N=p+rq,\qquad p,q\in\mathbb{P},\quad r\in\{1\}\cup\mathbb{P},\quad r\leq q^{a-% 1}.

Li and Liu take a=1.9a=1.9. Here a=1.8=9/5a=1.8=9/5, so r≤qa−1=q4/5=q0.8r\leq q^{a-1}=q^{4/5}=q^{0.8}. Theorem 1 follows from the strict comparison

Dlower\displaystyle D_{\rm lower} ≥1.83399665352036682372,\displaystyle\geq 1.83399665352036682372,
T\displaystyle T =8⁢log⁡5000939991<1.78838848345960807362<Dlower.\displaystyle=8\log\frac{50009}{39991}<1.78838848345960807362<D_{\rm lower}.

It holds at the fixed source cutoff below. We use the Chen-constant normalization

C⁢(N)=∏ℓ>2(1−1(ℓ−1)2)⁢∏ℓ∣Nℓ>2ℓ−1ℓ−2,UC=C⁢(N)⁢N(log⁡N)2;C(N)=\prod_{\ell>2}\left(1-\frac{1}{(\ell-1)^{2}}\right)\prod_{\begin{subarray% }{c}\ell\mid N\\ \ell>2\end{subarray}}\frac{\ell-1}{\ell-2},\qquad U_{C}=\frac{C(N)N}{(\log N)^% {2}};

There is no leading factor of two. With εA=10−4\varepsilon_{A}=10^{-4}, our selected endpoint and the pointwise division by four give

P2,εA⁢(N)≥[1.833813253855014787037628−o⁢(1)]⁢C⁢(N)⁢N/(log⁡N)2,P_{2,\varepsilon_{A}}(N)\geq[1.833813253855014787037628-o(1)]C(N)N/(\log N)^{2},

where P2,εA⁢(N)=#⁢{p<(1−εA)⁢N:p∈ℙ,Ω⁢(N−p)≤2}P_{2,\varepsilon_{A}}(N)=\#\{p<(1-\varepsilon_{A})N:p\in\mathbb{P},\ \Omega(N-% p)\leq 2\}. Our normalization uses C⁢(N)C(N) without a leading factor 22, as do Wu’s lower bounds D1,2⁢(N)≥0.836⁢C⁢(N)⁢N/(log⁡N)2D_{1,2}(N)\geq 0.836C(N)N/(\log N)^{2} [3, Theorem 2] and D1,2⁢(N)≥0.899⁢C⁢(N)⁢N/(log⁡N)2D_{1,2}(N)\geq 0.899C(N)N/(\log N)^{2} [4]. Here DlowerD_{\rm lower} is in D units. The source mass is 4⁢(1−εA)⁢UC4(1-\varepsilon_{A})U_{C}, so pointwise division by four contributes the factor 1−εA1-\varepsilon_{A} to DlowerD_{\rm lower}. Li–Liu’s (1+1.9)(1+1.9) argument uses the same singular-series convention and the corresponding limiting exclusion threshold 8⁢log⁡(10/9)=0.8428841252626104⁢…≈0.842888\log(10/9)=0.8428841252626104\ldots\approx 0.84288 [6, (5.42)–(5.43)].

1.1. Statement and sources

B.3. Source and interval references

The source identity is Lemma 2.1, with its prefix and sifting data kept fixed. Section 6 bounds both difference weights, including the G1 representation multiplicities.

Hypothesis (5.23) follows from the Prime interval coefficients lemma in Section 5. Its endpoint power-log Siegel–Walfisz input is [Z1, (2.21)]. Endpoint subtraction requires

Appendix C Finite source checks

Here we check source identities and cutoffs on selected instances. The main text proves these estimates uniformly in NN.

The script uses integer arithmetic and fractions.Fraction, with a smallest-prime-factor sieve through 400000400000. For each seed

1,2,20261022,1,\qquad 2,\qquad 20261022,

the script runs with second argument 150150 and Python random.Random(seed). It draws 150150 even integers N=2⋅randrange⁢(5000,60000)N=2\cdot\texttt{randrange}(5000,60000). Each draw selects z∈{5,7,11,13,17}z\in\{5,7,11,13,17\} and V0∈{200,500,1000,2000}V_{0}\in\{200,500,1000,2000\}. For each of the three prefix families below, it draws D∈{200,1000,5000}D\in\{200,1000,5000\} separately. It tests the primes vv with 100⁢v<99⁢N100v<99N. The plain sample also requires v>V0v>V_{0}. There are three prefix families: b=1b=1; the first at most six primes p∈[z,4⁢z)p\in[z,4z), p∤Np\nmid N; and the first at most six ordered pairs (p1,p2)(p_{1},p_{2}). The pairs satisfy z≤p2<p1<6⁢zz\leq p_{2}<p_{1}<6z and pi∤Np_{i}\nmid N. Thus the tested prefix condition is pi≥zp_{i}\geq z and (pi,N)=1(p_{i},N)=1.

For the three-step Buchstab identity, each seed gives 3030 further even integers N=2⋅randrange⁢(3000,15000)N=2\cdot\texttt{randrange}(3000,15000). Here z0=5z_{0}=5, z1∈{17,23,29}z_{1}\in\{17,23,29\} and V0=300V_{0}=300. The plain primes satisfy V0<vV_{0}<v and 100⁢v<99⁢N100v<99N. The switched checks use 3030 further even integers N=2⋅randrange⁢(20000,100000)N=2\cdot\texttt{randrange}(20000,100000). Set y1∈{5,7,11}y_{1}\in\{5,7,11\}, zsw∈{7,11,13}z_{\rm sw}\in\{7,11,13\}, and interval endpoints N/100,99⁢N/100N/100,99N/100. The ordered triples satisfy y1≤p1<p2≤p3y_{1}\leq p_{1}<p_{2}\leq p_{3}, p13<Np_{1}^{3}<N, p1⁢p22<Np_{1}p_{2}^{2}<N and N/100<p1⁢p2⁢p3<NN/100<p_{1}p_{2}p_{3}<N, with the coordinate bounds pi3<8⁢Np_{i}^{3}<8N. The tagged triples also have pi∤Np_{i}\nmid N and p3≠p2p_{3}\neq p_{2}. In these three batches the rational cutoffs are compared by cross-multiplying integers.

Each direct-row run has 450 batches. Together they contain 3,988,123 ambient tuples, and D2 and D4 report the combined counts. In D4, an “escape” is a tuple missed by the earlier difference predicates. Its cofactor has a sieving prime below zz, coprime to NN. The Buchstab and G1 counts also combine the three seeds. G1 counts coordinate-divisibility tags and repeated-prime tags separately, using a first-true partition: a coordinate-divisibility tag takes precedence over a repeated-prime tag when both predicates hold.

Each seed also gives five small examples. One further illustration has about 260 digits. The large examples use fixed-base Miller–Rabin screens. Their primality is uncertified. They illustrate the cutoffs only; neither the proof nor the numerical bounds use them.
